labels.name: Input Processing Weaknesses
labels.description: Root family for vulnerabilities caused by unsafe interpretation, transformation, routing, or storage of attacker-influenced input. Every descendant represents a more specific way in which externally controlled data crosses an intended processing boundary.

labels.name: Interpreter Injection
labels.description: Input-processing weaknesses in which attacker-controlled data changes the syntax or semantics consumed by an interpreter. Descendants distinguish the interpreter and construction mechanism rather than the eventual impact of execution.

labels.name: Query-Language Injection
labels.description: Interpreter injection in which untrusted data changes a structured query sent to a database, directory, or document-selection engine. The defect must alter query meaning rather than merely provide an unexpected query value.

labels.name: SQL Injection
labels.description: Attacker-controlled data is incorporated into SQL syntax without safe parameterization or equivalent separation, allowing the database statement structure or operations to be changed.

labels.name: NoSQL Query Injection
labels.description: Attacker-controlled data changes the operators, selectors, or executable structure of a non-relational database query, rather than being treated only as a literal stored or compared value.

labels.name: LDAP Injection
labels.description: Untrusted data changes an LDAP search filter or directory operation because filter metacharacters or query fragments are not safely separated from literal values.

labels.name: XPath or XQuery Injection
labels.description: Untrusted data changes an XPath or XQuery expression, enabling unintended document selection, predicate bypass, or query execution within an XML-oriented data engine.

labels.name: Command Construction Injection
labels.description: Interpreter injection caused while constructing an operating-system command or process invocation from attacker-controlled data. Descendants distinguish shell syntax injection from unsafe argument construction.

labels.name: Operating-System Command Injection
labels.description: Untrusted data becomes shell or command-interpreter syntax, allowing the attacker to introduce commands, pipelines, substitutions, redirections, or other executable shell constructs.

labels.name: Process Argument Injection
labels.description: A process is launched without shell-syntax injection, but attacker-controlled values become unintended command-line options or arguments that alter the invoked program's security-sensitive behavior.

labels.name: Dynamic Code Evaluation Injection
labels.description: Interpreter injection in which attacker-controlled content reaches a code, expression, or template evaluator. Descendants distinguish direct source-code evaluation from specialized expression and template languages.

labels.name: Direct Code Injection
labels.description: Attacker-supplied source code or code fragments are directly evaluated by a general-purpose runtime such as PHP, Python, JavaScript, Ruby, or a comparable language interpreter.

labels.name: Expression-Language Injection
labels.description: Attacker-controlled data changes an application expression evaluated by a dedicated expression language, such as OGNL, SpEL, or EL, without requiring direct general-purpose source-code input.

labels.name: Server-Side Template Injection
labels.description: Attacker-controlled template syntax is evaluated by a server-side template engine, exposing template operations or underlying runtime capabilities beyond intended literal rendering.

labels.name: Browser Content Injection
labels.description: Input-processing weaknesses in which untrusted content is inserted into a browser-consumed document or style context without the contextual encoding or structural separation required by that context.

labels.name: Cross-Site Scripting
labels.description: Attacker-controlled script-capable content is inserted into a web page and executes in another user's browser origin because the application or client library fails to neutralize the relevant HTML or script context.

labels.name: Non-Script HTML Injection
labels.description: Attacker-controlled markup changes visible page structure, forms, or navigation without evidence that script executes. Use this only when the defining property is unauthorized HTML structure rather than XSS.

labels.name: CSS Injection
labels.description: Attacker-controlled data becomes stylesheet syntax and changes rendering or data-selection behavior in a browser without requiring the injected content to execute as JavaScript.

labels.name: Path and Resource Selection Weaknesses
labels.description: Input-processing weaknesses in which attacker-controlled names, paths, links, or archive entries select a filesystem resource outside the location intended by the application.

labels.name: Path Traversal
labels.description: Attacker-controlled path components, encoded separators, or normalization edge cases resolve outside an intended directory and allow access to a filesystem resource beyond the authorized path scope.

labels.name: Archive Extraction Path Traversal
labels.description: A crafted archive entry contains an absolute or traversing path that escapes the extraction directory when unpacked, causing files to be read or written outside the intended archive destination.

labels.name: Improper Symbolic-Link Resolution
labels.description: The application follows or replaces symbolic links, junctions, or equivalent filesystem references without ensuring that the resolved resource remains inside the authorized boundary.

labels.name: Unrestricted Filename Control
labels.description: Attacker-controlled filenames select or overwrite unintended resources even though directory traversal is not the established mechanism, such as collision with a security-sensitive fixed-location file.

labels.name: Unsafe Structured-Data Processing
labels.description: Input-processing weaknesses caused when structured objects, documents, or property graphs are reconstructed or interpreted with capabilities that exceed the intended data-only contract.

labels.name: Deserialization of Untrusted Data
labels.description: Attacker-controlled serialized data is restored into objects without adequate type or behavior restrictions, enabling gadget invocation, unsafe object construction, or security-sensitive state manipulation.

labels.name: XML External Entity Expansion
labels.description: An XML parser processes attacker-controlled external entity declarations or references, permitting unintended local-file access, network requests, or disclosure through entity resolution.

labels.name: Prototype Pollution
labels.description: Attacker-controlled object properties modify a shared prototype or inheritance structure, causing later property lookups or object behavior to use unauthorized values.

labels.name: Unsafe Mass Assignment
labels.description: A framework binds untrusted structured input to object fields without an allowlist, letting the attacker set security-sensitive properties that were not intended to be externally writable.

labels.name: Network Routing and Destination Control
labels.description: Input-processing weaknesses in which attacker-controlled network identifiers cause a server, intermediary, or client to use an unintended destination or routing context.

labels.name: Server-Side Request Forgery
labels.description: Attacker-controlled input coerces the vulnerable server into issuing a request to an unintended internal or external resource using the server's network position or credentials.

labels.name: Unvalidated Redirect
labels.description: Attacker-controlled destination data causes an application response to redirect a user's client to an unintended external location without an adequate destination allowlist.

labels.name: Host Header Injection
labels.description: An untrusted HTTP Host or forwarded-host value controls security-sensitive URL generation, tenant routing, password-reset links, or backend selection without authoritative host validation.

labels.name: File Upload Control Weaknesses
labels.description: Input-processing weaknesses in which externally supplied files are accepted, named, typed, or stored without the restrictions required by the upload feature's security boundary.

labels.name: Unrestricted File Upload
labels.description: An upload endpoint accepts attacker-controlled files without the access, type, or policy restriction fundamental to the feature, allowing arbitrary content to be placed through an otherwise exposed upload workflow.

labels.name: Dangerous File-Type Upload
labels.description: An upload feature exists legitimately but its type validation permits executable, active, or otherwise dangerous content that the surrounding deployment may process with security-sensitive behavior.

labels.name: Upload Destination Control
labels.description: An attacker can choose an unauthorized storage destination for an uploaded file even though the upload itself is permitted, without relying on archive extraction or generic path traversal.

labels.name: Identity and Access Control Weaknesses
labels.description: Root family for vulnerabilities caused by failures to establish identity, maintain an authenticated session, or authorize a security-sensitive action or resource. Descendants specialize the failed access-control decision.

labels.name: Authentication Weaknesses
labels.description: Access-control weaknesses that prevent the system from reliably establishing or recovering a principal's identity before granting the authenticated security context.

labels.name: Broken Authentication
labels.description: The primary authentication mechanism can be bypassed or subverted because credential verification, identity binding, or authentication-state establishment is implemented incorrectly.

labels.name: Weak Password Recovery
labels.description: An account-recovery workflow authenticates the requester with guessable, exposed, replayable, or insufficient evidence and thereby permits unauthorized credential replacement.

labels.name: Authentication Bypass
labels.description: A reachable alternate path, parsing discrepancy, or logic condition skips a normally required authentication check and directly creates or accepts an authenticated context.

labels.name: Default Credentials
labels.description: The product grants an authenticated identity through factory credentials that are shared, predictable, or documented and remain active without a mandatory secure initialization step.

labels.name: Session Management Weaknesses
labels.description: Access-control weaknesses in the creation, binding, rotation, lifetime, or invalidation of an already authenticated session identifier or token.

labels.name: Session Fixation
labels.description: The application accepts or preserves a session identifier controlled by the attacker across authentication, allowing the attacker to reuse the victim's resulting authenticated session.

labels.name: Predictable Session Token
labels.description: Authenticated session identifiers can be feasibly predicted because their generation lacks sufficient entropy or exposes a deterministic relationship between tokens.

labels.name: Missing Session Expiration
labels.description: A session remains valid beyond its intended lifetime or after a security-sensitive invalidation event because expiration, logout, or revocation is not enforced.

labels.name: Authorization Weaknesses
labels.description: Access-control weaknesses in which an identified or anonymous principal can perform an action or access a resource outside the permissions intended for that principal.

labels.name: Improper Authorization
labels.description: A security-sensitive operation lacks an effective permission check or applies the wrong authorization policy, granting functionality or resources to a principal that should not receive them.

labels.name: Insecure Direct Object Reference
labels.description: An attacker changes an object identifier and accesses another principal's resource because object-level authorization is absent or is not bound to the requested identifier.

labels.name: Privilege Boundary Bypass
labels.description: An already recognized principal crosses an intended privilege boundary and obtains a more powerful role or execution context because the transition is not properly authorized.

labels.name: Missing Function-Level Authorization
labels.description: A privileged endpoint or operation is exposed to lower-privileged callers because access is checked only in the user interface or omitted from the server-side function.

labels.name: Request Authorization Weaknesses
labels.description: Access-control weaknesses where a request carries valid ambient authority but the application fails to establish that the authorized principal intentionally originated, approved, or freshly issued it.

labels.name: Cross-Site Request Forgery
labels.description: A cross-site attacker causes a victim's browser to submit a security-sensitive request with the victim's ambient credentials because the application does not verify request intent or origin.

labels.name: Improper CORS Origin Authorization
labels.description: A server authorizes a malicious or overly broad web origin to read credentialed cross-origin responses because its Access-Control-Allow-Origin decision is incorrectly validated.

labels.name: Authenticated Request Replay
labels.description: A previously valid authenticated request can be repeated to perform an additional unauthorized action because freshness, nonce, sequence, or one-time authorization is not enforced.

labels.name: Memory Safety Weaknesses
labels.description: Root family for vulnerabilities caused by invalid access to storage managed by a native or otherwise memory-unsafe runtime. Descendants distinguish spatial bounds, object initialization, type, and lifetime violations.

labels.name: Spatial Memory Safety
labels.description: Memory-safety weaknesses in which an access targets bytes outside the bounds of the object or region that the operation is allowed to read or write.

labels.name: Out-of-Bounds Write
labels.description: A write operation stores data outside the valid boundary of its destination object or allocation. Descendants identify common boundary-crossing write patterns.

labels.name: Buffer Overflow
labels.description: Data is copied, appended, or written past the capacity of a fixed-size stack, heap, or static buffer because the implementation fails to enforce the destination boundary.

labels.name: Off-by-One Write
labels.description: A boundary calculation permits exactly one element or byte to be written outside the valid destination region, commonly through an inclusive limit or terminator mistake.

labels.name: Invalid Integer-Indexed Write
labels.description: An unchecked, truncated, wrapped, or signed index selects a write location outside an allocated object without the evidence specifically establishing a sequential buffer-overflow operation.

labels.name: Out-of-Bounds Read
labels.description: A read operation accesses bytes outside the valid boundary of an allocated object, buffer, or region and may disclose adjacent process memory or influence execution with unintended values.

labels.name: Invalid Pointer Read
labels.description: The program dereferences an invalid non-null pointer and reads from an unauthorized or unmapped address, without evidence that the access is specifically past a known object's boundary.

labels.name: Memory Initialization Weaknesses
labels.description: Memory-safety weaknesses in which storage or a pointer is used before the implementation establishes the valid initialized state required by the operation.

labels.name: Uninitialized Memory Read
labels.description: The program reads bytes whose value has not been initialized for the current object or operation, potentially disclosing prior contents or making control decisions from indeterminate data.

labels.name: Null Pointer Dereference
labels.description: The program dereferences a null pointer because a required object or error condition was not checked. Select this mechanism rather than a generic denial-of-service consequence.

labels.name: Uninitialized Pointer Use
labels.description: A pointer value is consumed before being assigned a valid target, causing memory access through an indeterminate address rather than through a stale freed object.

labels.name: Temporal Memory Safety
labels.description: Memory-safety weaknesses caused by using, releasing, or reusing an object outside the valid lifetime established by its allocation and ownership rules.

labels.name: Use After Free
labels.description: The program accesses an object after its storage has been released, so subsequent allocation or attacker influence can replace the expected object contents or metadata.

labels.name: Double Free
labels.description: The same allocation is released more than once without an intervening valid allocation, corrupting allocator state or allowing later memory manipulation.

labels.name: Dangling Pointer Use
labels.description: A pointer remains reachable after its target object's lifetime ends and is later dereferenced, including non-heap lifetime errors not more specifically established as use-after-free.

labels.name: Stale Handle Use
labels.description: A recycled or invalidated numeric handle, descriptor, or object token is reused and resolves to a different resource after the original resource lifetime has ended.

labels.name: Memory Object Type Safety
labels.description: Memory-safety weaknesses in which storage is interpreted as an incompatible object type, layout, or runtime variant and the resulting access violates the object's valid representation.

labels.name: Type Confusion
labels.description: The program treats an object as a different runtime type than the object actually has, causing field, method, or layout access under incompatible assumptions.

labels.name: Invalid Object Downcast
labels.description: An unchecked or incorrect cast narrows an object to an incompatible subtype and subsequent native access relies on fields or layout that the original object does not provide.

labels.name: Variant Discriminator Mismatch
labels.description: A union, tagged variant, or equivalent structure is accessed through a member inconsistent with its active discriminator, producing invalid object interpretation or memory access.

labels.name: Availability and Resource Management Weaknesses
labels.description: Root family for vulnerabilities whose defining defect is uncontrolled consumption, retention, coordination, or amplification of finite computational resources. Incidental crashes caused by another weakness family are excluded.

labels.name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
labels.description: Availability weaknesses in which attacker-triggered work, objects, processes, or requests consume a finite resource without an effective per-client, per-operation, or global bound.

labels.name: Generic Resource Exhaustion
labels.description: Attacker-controlled operations consume CPU, memory, bandwidth, stream state, or another finite resource at an unbounded rate, causing service degradation or denial of service without a more specific descendant mechanism.

labels.name: Algorithmic Complexity Attack
labels.description: Crafted input triggers pathologically expensive algorithmic behavior, such as excessive backtracking, collision handling, or superlinear parsing, and thereby exhausts computation.

labels.name: Uncontrolled Recursion
labels.description: Attacker-influenced nesting or cyclic input causes recursion without an adequate depth or cycle bound, exhausting stack space or computation.

labels.name: Connection Pool Exhaustion
labels.description: An attacker can occupy or create connections faster than they are released because concurrency, lifetime, or per-client limits do not protect the finite connection pool.

labels.name: Unbounded Process or Thread Creation
labels.description: Attacker-triggered activity causes processes or threads to be created without an effective bound, exhausting scheduler, memory, identifier, or operating-system resources.

labels.name: Resource Lifecycle Weaknesses
labels.description: Availability weaknesses where resources acquired for completed or failed operations are not released according to their intended lifecycle and accumulate over time.

labels.name: Memory Leak
labels.description: Allocated memory remains reachable or reserved after it is no longer needed because a release path, ownership transfer, or cleanup operation is missing.

labels.name: Unbounded Memory Allocation
labels.description: Attacker-controlled sizes or object counts cause new memory allocations without an effective upper bound, regardless of whether each allocation would later be correctly released.

labels.name: File Descriptor Leak
labels.description: Files, sockets, pipes, or comparable operating-system handles are repeatedly opened but not closed on one or more reachable paths, eventually exhausting descriptor capacity.

labels.name: Availability Coordination Failures
labels.description: Availability weaknesses where concurrent actors cannot make progress because locking, retry, or coordination rules create a stable non-progress condition or self-amplifying workload.

labels.name: Deadlock
labels.description: Two or more execution contexts wait indefinitely for resources or conditions held by one another because the locking or acquisition order permits a circular dependency.

labels.name: Livelock
labels.description: Execution contexts remain active and repeatedly react to one another but cannot complete useful work because their coordination protocol continually changes or retries state.

labels.name: Unbounded Retry Amplification
labels.description: A failure or attacker-controlled response causes clients or workers to retry without sufficient limits, delay, or deduplication, amplifying load and preventing recovery.

labels.name: Cryptographic Protection Weaknesses
labels.description: Root family for vulnerabilities caused by incorrect selection, construction, validation, randomness, or key management in a cryptographic security control. Merely handling plaintext outside such a control is not sufficient.

labels.name: Cryptographic Algorithm Selection
labels.description: Cryptographic weaknesses caused by choosing an algorithm, primitive, mode, parameter size, or construction that does not provide the security property claimed by the control.

labels.name: Weak Cryptographic Construction
labels.description: The implemented cryptographic construction is known to provide inadequate confidentiality, integrity, or authenticity for the stated threat model, without a more specific descendant selection defect.

labels.name: Deprecated Cipher or Mode
labels.description: A deprecated encryption algorithm or mode remains enabled even though practical weaknesses make it unsuitable for protecting the data or protocol in which it is used.

labels.name: Weak Cryptographic Hash
labels.description: A hash with inadequate collision, preimage, or password-resistance properties is used for a security-sensitive integrity, signature, credential, or identity purpose.

labels.name: Insufficient Cryptographic Key Length
labels.description: A cryptographic key or modulus is configured with a size that permits feasible brute force or cryptanalysis for the required protection lifetime.

labels.name: Cryptographic Key Management
labels.description: Cryptographic weaknesses in generation, storage, distribution, separation, rotation, or reuse of secret key material rather than in the selected primitive itself.

labels.name: Hard-Coded Cryptographic Key
labels.description: Secret cryptographic key material is embedded identically in software or firmware and therefore becomes recoverable and shared across installations or protected objects.

labels.name: Insecure Key Storage
labels.description: Secret key material is stored with protections that do not match the local attacker or tenant threat model, allowing unauthorized principals to retrieve or replace it.

labels.name: Predictable Cryptographic Key
labels.description: Key generation uses predictable state, insufficient entropy, or attacker-influenced values so that an adversary can reconstruct or narrow the generated secret.

labels.name: Unsafe Cryptographic Key Reuse
labels.description: The same key material is reused across contexts, tenants, purposes, or epochs whose separation is required for the cryptographic construction's security guarantees.

labels.name: Randomness and Nonce Weaknesses
labels.description: Cryptographic weaknesses caused by predictable, repeated, biased, or insufficiently large random values, tokens, initialization vectors, salts, or nonces.

labels.name: Insufficient Randomness
labels.description: A security-sensitive random value is generated from a source or transformation with insufficient entropy for the attacker's observation and prediction capabilities.

labels.name: Predictable Security Token
labels.description: A password-reset, invitation, anti-replay, or other security token can be feasibly predicted because token generation exposes deterministic or low-entropy structure.

labels.name: Cryptographic Nonce Reuse
labels.description: A cryptographic construction receives a nonce, IV, or ephemeral value that repeats under the same key even though uniqueness is required for confidentiality, integrity, or signature security.

labels.name: Certificate and Peer Validation
labels.description: Cryptographic weaknesses where a secure-channel client or verifier fails to establish that the presented certificate and peer identity satisfy the intended trust policy.

labels.name: Improper Certificate Validation
labels.description: Certificate chain, signature, trust anchor, constraints, or validity requirements are not correctly verified before accepting the peer's authenticated identity.

labels.name: Missing Hostname Validation
labels.description: A certificate chain may be trusted, but the verifier does not confirm that the certificate identity matches the hostname or service identity requested by the client.

labels.name: Expired Certificate Acceptance
labels.description: The verifier accepts a certificate outside its validity interval despite the trust policy requiring current validity at the time of the connection or signed operation.

labels.name: Deployment and Information-Handling Weaknesses
labels.description: Root family for vulnerabilities caused by insecure deployment state or direct mishandling of sensitive information. Descendants exclude disclosures that are merely consequences of a separately established injection, traversal, or memory-safety defect.

labels.name: Insecure Deployment State
labels.description: Deployment weaknesses where enabled services, permissions, defaults, or isolation settings create an exposure that is not inherent to the correctly configured product behavior.

labels.name: Insecure Defaults
labels.description: A fresh or ordinary deployment enables a security-sensitive capability or permissive policy by default without requiring an explicit risk-accepting administrator decision.

labels.name: Excessive Deployment Permissions
labels.description: Installed files, processes, service accounts, or runtime resources receive broader operating-system or platform permissions than the documented feature requires.

labels.name: Security Feature Disabled
labels.description: A deployment omits or disables an available security control that the product's intended threat model requires, such as authentication, sandboxing, isolation, or transport protection.

labels.name: Exposed Service Surface
labels.description: Deployment weaknesses where a diagnostic, administrative, development, or unnecessary service is reachable by principals outside its intended operational audience.

labels.name: Exposed Debug Interface
labels.description: A debugging endpoint, console, protocol, or diagnostic capability is reachable in deployment and grants observation or control intended only for trusted development use.

labels.name: Exposed Administrative Interface
labels.description: A management interface is reachable from an unauthorized network or tenant boundary even though it was intended for a restricted administrative plane.

labels.name: Directory Listing Enabled
labels.description: The deployed web or file service enumerates directory contents to unauthorized users because automatic index generation or browsing remains enabled.

labels.name: Unnecessary Service Enabled
labels.description: A service or protocol not required for the deployment's intended function remains enabled and exposes additional reachable attack surface.

labels.name: Direct Sensitive-Information Handling
labels.description: Information-handling weaknesses where the application directly emits, stores, or transmits sensitive data through an unintended channel, rather than disclosure arising only after exploiting another weakness family.

labels.name: Diagnostic or Metadata Information Exposure
labels.description: Errors, diagnostics, headers, or metadata directly reveal sensitive technical or user information that the normal response contract should not expose. Secondary disclosure from traversal or memory over-read is excluded.

labels.name: Sensitive Data in Logs
labels.description: The application writes credentials, tokens, personal data, cryptographic material, or comparable secrets into logs accessible beyond the data's intended audience.

labels.name: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Data
labels.description: Sensitive information is persistently stored without the confidentiality protection required against principals who can access the storage medium or backing service.

labels.name: Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Data
labels.description: Sensitive information is transmitted over a channel without the confidentiality protection required against network observers or intermediaries in the stated threat model.

labels.name: Cross-Tenant Data Leakage
labels.description: A cache, shared state, response mix-up, or tenant-context error directly returns one tenant's data to another without requiring a separate object-identifier authorization bypass.
